# The exemption taxonomy

Every redaction this tool proposes carries one of the codes below, and every code
is tied to a provision of a real statute. The codes are the closed set: the
decision layer cannot invent a category, and a span it cannot place lands on an
escalation code rather than on a guess.

**This is not legal advice and not a legal determination.** The mapping is a
proposal a reviewer applies. A public body brings its own interpretation, and the
mapping is a YAML file precisely so that it can.

Generated 2026-10-08 from `sever/taxonomy/`, the date of its last update.

## The codes

| Code | Decision | Category |
|---|---|---|
| `R1` | Redact | Third-party personal information |
| `R2` | Redact | Mixed span, third-party information entangled with the requester's |
| `K1` | Keep | The requester's own personal information |
| `K2` | Keep | An official of a public body acting in that capacity |
| `K3` | Keep | Already publicly available |
| `K4` | Keep | An individual dead more than twenty years |
| `K5` | Keep | Consent given, or a discretionary benefit of a financial nature |
| `K6` | Keep | Not personal information |
| `E1` | Escalate | Role undeterminable from the record |
| `E2` | Escalate | Mixed span the rules cannot sever cleanly |
| `E3` | Flag only | Candidate non-personal exemption |

Escalation withholds. An undecided span is proposed for redaction and flagged for
the reviewer, never released on the assumption that it was probably fine.

## What each code means

### `R1`: Third-party personal information

**Redact.** Personal information about an identifiable individual who is not the requester and who is not an officer, employee or contractor of a public body acting in that capacity. A professional who does not work for the public body, such as a physician, lawyer or counsellor writing about a client, is a third party even in their professional role: the exclusion for officials covers public bodies' own people and nobody else. Identity, contact details, identifiers, health, financial, educational, criminal or employment history, and the views or opinions of others about them.

*The question behind it:* Is this individual a third party, and is the information about them personal rather than about the functions of a position they hold?

Examples:

- The complainant's home address in a case note.
- A member of the public's date of birth in an incident report.
- A named neighbour's account of what they saw.

Traps:

- An official who is also a complainant in the same record is a third party in that capacity: their complaint is personal information even though their job title is not.

*Canada (federal):*

| Provision | Heading | Verification | Text or reason |
|---|---|---|---|
| Access to Information Act, s. 19(1) | Personal information | checked 2026-09-13 | "Subject to subsection (2), the head of a government institution shall refuse to disclose any record requested under this Part that contains personal information." |
| Privacy Act, s. 3 | Definition of personal information | checked 2026-09-13 | "personal information means information about an identifiable individual that is recorded in any form." |

> Section 19 of the Act imports the Privacy Act definition wholesale, so the question the tool actually answers for R1 is the definitional one: is there an identifiable individual, and is the information about them.

*Newfoundland and Labrador:*

| Provision | Heading | Verification | Text or reason |
|---|---|---|---|
| Access to Information and Protection of Privacy Act, 2015, s. 40(1) | Disclosure harmful to personal privacy | checked 2026-09-13 | "The head of a public body shall refuse to disclose personal information to an applicant where the disclosure would be an unreasonable invasion of a third party's personal privacy." |
| Access to Information and Protection of Privacy Act, 2015, s. 2 | Definition of personal information | checked 2026-09-20 | ""personal information" means recorded information about an identifiable individual, including (i) the individual's name, address or telephone number, (ii) the individual's race, national or ethnic origin, colour, or religious or political beliefs or associations, (iii) the individual's age, sex, sexual orientation, marital status or family status, (iv) an identifying number, symbol or other particular assigned to the individual, (v) the individual's fingerprints, blood type or inheritable characteristics, (vi) information about the individual's health care status or history, including a physical or mental disability, (vii) information about the individual's educational, financial, criminal or employment status or history, (viii) the opinions of a person about the individual, and (ix) the individual's personal views or opinions, except where they are about someone else" |

> The NL test is different in kind from the federal one and the difference matters. Federally, section 19 refuses disclosure of personal information as such. Here the refusal is triggered by an "unreasonable invasion" of privacy, section 40(4) sets out presumptions of unreasonable invasion and section 40(5) sets out the factors to weigh. A single R1 code cannot carry that weighing, so under this configuration R1 means "presumptively an unreasonable invasion, for the reviewer to weigh", and docs/escalation.md records that the tool does not perform the section 40(5) balance.

### `R2`: Mixed span, third-party information entangled with the requester's

**Redact.** A span in which a third party's personal information cannot be separated from the requester's own without severing inside the span. The third party's part is withheld; the remainder of the record is released.

*The question behind it:* Can this span be severed so the requester keeps their own information and the third party keeps their privacy?

Examples:

- "Ms Okonkwo told the investigator that Mr Byrne had shouted at her", on a request made by Mr Byrne.

Traps:

- Severing the whole sentence over-redacts the requester's own information; severing nothing leaks the third party's.

*Canada (federal):*

| Provision | Heading | Verification | Text or reason |
|---|---|---|---|
| Access to Information Act, s. 25 | Severability | checked 2026-09-13 | "where a request is made to a government institution for access to a record that the head of the institution is authorized to refuse to disclose under this Part by reason of information or other material contained in the record, the head of the institution shall disclose any part of the record that does not contain, and can reasonably be severed from any part that contains, any such information or material." |
| Access to Information Act, s. 19(1) | Personal information | checked 2026-09-13 | "Subject to subsection (2), the head of a government institution shall refuse to disclose any record requested under this Part that contains personal information." |

> R2 exists because section 25 makes severance mandatory, not optional. Withholding a whole sentence to protect one name in it is a section 25 failure, and it is the failure this project measures as over-redaction.

*Newfoundland and Labrador:*

| Provision | Heading | Verification | Text or reason |
|---|---|---|---|
| Access to Information and Protection of Privacy Act, 2015, s. 8(2) | Right of access, severance | checked 2026-09-13 | "The right of access to a record does not extend to information excepted from disclosure under this Act, but if it is reasonable to sever that information from the record, an applicant has a right of access to the remainder of the record." |
| Access to Information and Protection of Privacy Act, 2015, s. 40(1) | Disclosure harmful to personal privacy | checked 2026-09-13 | "The head of a public body shall refuse to disclose personal information to an applicant where the disclosure would be an unreasonable invasion of a third party's personal privacy." |

### `K1`: The requester's own personal information

**Keep.** Personal information about the individual who made the request. It is released to them. This is the single most consequential keep: a tool that redacts a requester's own information from their own file has failed at the thing they asked for.

*The question behind it:* Does this information belong to the requester as configured for this request?

Examples:

- The requester's own address, file number, medical detail or stated opinion.

Traps:

- The requester mentioned as a witness to someone else's matter is still the requester; the span stays.
- A requester's name appearing inseparably next to a third party's is R2, not K1.

*Canada (federal):*

| Provision | Heading | Verification | Text or reason |
|---|---|---|---|
| Privacy Act, s. 12(1) | Right of access | checked 2026-09-13 | "Subject to this Act, every individual who is a Canadian citizen or a permanent resident within the meaning of subsection 2(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act has a right to and shall, on request, be given access to (a) any personal information about the individual contained in a personal information bank." |

> Federally this is the one code whose anchor sits outside the Access to Information Act. A requester's own personal information is still "personal information" for section 19, so on a pure Access to Information Act request it is technically exempt; the right of access to one's own information lives in section 12 of the Privacy Act and such requests are handled there. The tool proposes K1 because the releasing analyst is almost always working a combined or a Privacy Act file, and because redacting a requester's own information from their own record is the failure that makes a tool useless. A public body that wants the strict Access to Information Act reading sets keep_requester_information to false in the request configuration and K1 becomes R1.

*Newfoundland and Labrador:*

| Provision | Heading | Verification | Text or reason |
|---|---|---|---|
| Access to Information and Protection of Privacy Act, 2015, s. 8(1) | Right of access | checked 2026-09-13 | "A person who makes a request under section 11 has a right of access to a record in the custody or under the control of a public body, including a record containing personal information about the applicant." |

> Cleaner than the federal position: the NL right of access expressly includes the applicant's own personal information in the same section, and section 40 protects a third party's privacy rather than personal information at large. K1 needs no configuration switch under this jurisdiction.

### `K2`: An official of a public body acting in that capacity

**Keep.** Information about an officer or employee of a public body, or an individual performing services under contract, that relates to the position or the functions of the position: the fact of employment, name, title, business address and telephone number, classification and salary range, the name on a document they prepared in the course of employment, and opinions or views they gave in the course of employment.

*The question behind it:* Is this about the person, or about the job they were doing when they did it?

Examples:

- The signature block of the officer who wrote the letter.
- A manager's recommendation in a briefing note, given in the course of duty.

Traps:

- An official's personal mobile number or home address is not about the position.
- An official's own grievance or medical leave is not about the position.

*Canada (federal):*

| Provision | Heading | Verification | Text or reason |
|---|---|---|---|
| Privacy Act, s. 3(j) | Exclusion, officers and employees of a government institution | checked 2026-09-13 | "information about an individual who is or was an officer or employee of a government institution that relates to the position or functions of the individual." |
| Privacy Act, s. 3(k) | Exclusion, individuals performing services under contract | checked 2026-09-13 | "information about an individual who is or was performing services under contract for a government institution that relates to the services performed." |
| Privacy Act, s. 3(j.1) | Exclusion, ministerial advisers and staff | checked 2026-09-20 | "the fact that an individual is or was a ministerial adviser or a member of a ministerial staff, as those terms are defined in subsection 2(1) of the Conflict of Interest Act, as well as the individual's name and title," |

> The exclusion is expressly limited to sections 7, 8 and 26 of the Privacy Act and section 19 of the Access to Information Act. That is the section this tool operates under, so the exclusion applies. The words that do the work are "relates to the position or functions": an official's own grievance, medical leave or home address does not, and is R1.

*Newfoundland and Labrador:*

| Provision | Heading | Verification | Text or reason |
|---|---|---|---|
| Access to Information and Protection of Privacy Act, 2015, s. 40(2)(f) | Exception, position, functions or remuneration of a public body officer | checked 2026-09-20 | "the information is about a third party's position, functions or remuneration as an officer, employee or member of a public body or as a member of a minister's staff" |
| Access to Information and Protection of Privacy Act, 2015, s. 40(2)(g) | Exception, details of a contract to supply goods or services | checked 2026-09-20 | "the disclosure reveals financial and other details of a contract to supply goods or services to a public body" |
| Access to Information and Protection of Privacy Act, 2015, s. 40(2)(h) | Exception, opinions given in the course of performing services | checked 2026-09-20 | "the disclosure reveals the opinions or views of a third party given in the course of performing services for a public body, except where they are given in respect of another individual" |

> This was the largest open item in the NL mapping and the code the whole over-redaction number turns on, so the letters were confirmed against the consolidated text rather than guessed: (f), (g) and (h), on 2026-09-20. Paragraph (h) carries a limit that K2 does not encode and a reviewer has to apply: an opinion given in the course of performing services is not an unreasonable invasion "except where they are given in respect of another individual". An official's assessment of a member of the public is outside the exception, so K2 is wrong for it and the span is R1. The tool does not detect that distinction and docs/escalation.md records it.

### `K3`: Already publicly available

**Keep.** Personal information that is already public: a minister or deputy head named in a published list, a name on the record's own letterhead, an individual named in a published organisation chart or a public register.

*The question behind it:* Is this already published somewhere a member of the public can read it?

Examples:

- The name of the minister in the address block of a letter.

Traps:

- Widely known inside the department is not the same as publicly available.

*Canada (federal):*

| Provision | Heading | Verification | Text or reason |
|---|---|---|---|
| Access to Information Act, s. 19(2)(b) | Where disclosure authorized, publicly available | checked 2026-09-13 | "The head of a government institution may disclose any record requested under this Part that contains personal information if the information is publicly available." |

> Subsection 19(2) is discretionary ("may disclose"), so K3 is a proposal to exercise a discretion, not a statement that the head must. The reviewer holds the discretion; the tool supplies the register match that makes it available.

*Newfoundland and Labrador:*

| Provision | Heading | Verification | Text or reason |
|---|---|---|---|
| Access to Information and Protection of Privacy Act, 2015, s. 40(2)(m) | Exception, attendance at a public event and receipt of an honour | checked 2026-09-20 | "the disclosure is not contrary to the public interest as described in subsection (3) and reveals only the following personal information about a third party: (i) attendance at or participation in a public event or activity related to a public body, including a graduation ceremony, sporting event, cultural program or club, or field trip, or (ii) receipt of an honour or award granted by or through a public body" |

> Checked on 2026-09-20, and the answer to the open question is that the NL Act has no general publicly-available exception in the terms of the federal 19(2)(b). Paragraph (m) is narrow: two enumerated situations, and only where the disclosure is not contrary to the public interest as described in subsection (3). So K3 does not mean under this jurisdiction what it means federally, and the difference is not cosmetic. A name that is already public for some other reason, published elsewhere or otherwise in the public domain is not released by paragraph (m). Under the NL configuration K3 covers the two enumerated situations only, and anything the detector reaches through general "already public" reasoning belongs in escalation. Recorded in docs/escalation.md.

### `K4`: An individual dead more than twenty years

**Keep.** Information about an individual who has been dead for more than twenty years is outside the definition of personal information.

*The question behind it:* Is the date of death in the record, and is it more than twenty years ago?

Examples:

- A historical file naming a person who died in 1968.

Traps:

- A date of death that is not in the record cannot be assumed. Absent a date in the record, this is E1, not K4.

*Canada (federal):*

| Provision | Heading | Verification | Text or reason |
|---|---|---|---|
| Privacy Act, s. 3(m) | Exclusion, individuals dead more than twenty years | checked 2026-09-13 | "information about an individual who has been dead for more than twenty years." |

*Newfoundland and Labrador:*

| Provision | Heading | Verification | Text or reason |
|---|---|---|---|
| Access to Information and Protection of Privacy Act, 2015, s. 40(5)(j) | Relevant circumstance, information about a deceased person | checked 2026-09-20 | "the information is about a deceased person and, if so, whether the length of time the person has been deceased indicates the disclosure is not an unreasonable invasion of the deceased person's personal privacy" |

> Confirmed on 2026-09-20, and the quote settles a question that was open. The federal Act excludes an individual dead more than twenty years from the definition of personal information outright. NL does not. Paragraph 40(5)(j) makes the length of time a relevant circumstance the head of a public body weighs, and it states no period at all. A K4 that releases on a fixed number of years is therefore wrong under this jurisdiction twice over: it performs a weighing the Act reserves to a person, and the threshold it weighs against is one this project invented. Under the NL configuration K4 routes to escalation. docs/escalation.md recorded this as an open taxonomy question; it is now a decided one.

### `K5`: Consent given, or a discretionary benefit of a financial nature

**Keep.** Information the individual has consented to disclose, and information relating to a discretionary benefit of a financial nature conferred on an individual, including the name of the individual and the exact nature of the benefit.

*The question behind it:* Is there consent on the file, or is this a licence, permit or grant the public body conferred?

Examples:

- The name of a grant recipient and the amount of the grant.

Traps:

- A benefit that is an entitlement rather than discretionary is not K5.

*Canada (federal):*

| Provision | Heading | Verification | Text or reason |
|---|---|---|---|
| Access to Information Act, s. 19(2)(a) | Where disclosure authorized, consent | checked 2026-09-13 | "The head of a government institution may disclose any record requested under this Part that contains personal information if the individual to whom it relates consents to the disclosure." |
| Privacy Act, s. 3(l) | Exclusion, discretionary benefit of a financial nature | checked 2026-09-13 | "information relating to any discretionary benefit of a financial nature, including the granting of a licence or permit, conferred on an individual, including the name of the individual and the exact nature of the benefit." |

> Two different mechanisms share one code because they share one reviewer question ("is there a reason on the file that this may be released"). The generated schedule cites whichever provision the rule fired on, not both.

*Newfoundland and Labrador:*

| Provision | Heading | Verification | Text or reason |
|---|---|---|---|
| Access to Information and Protection of Privacy Act, 2015, s. 40(2)(b) | Exception, the third party has consented in writing | checked 2026-09-20 | "the third party to whom the information relates has, in writing, consented to or requested the disclosure" |
| Access to Information and Protection of Privacy Act, 2015, s. 40(2)(l) | Exception, a discretionary benefit of a financial nature | checked 2026-09-20 | "the disclosure reveals details of a discretionary benefit of a financial nature granted to a third party by a public body, not including (i) personal information that is supplied in support of the application for the benefit, or (ii) personal information that relates to eligibility for income and employment support under the Income and Employment Support Act or to the determination of income or employment support levels" |

> Letters confirmed on 2026-09-20: (b) for consent, (l) for a discretionary benefit of a financial nature. Paragraph (l) carves out more than the federal equivalent and the carve-out is the part that matters. The information supplied in support of an application, and anything about eligibility for or the level of income and employment support, stays withheld. A record about a benefit is therefore usually a mixture, one part releasable under (l) and the rest not, and K5 cannot make that split. The tool proposes K5 for the fact and the amount of a discretionary benefit only.

### `K6`: Not personal information

**Keep.** The detector flagged a span that is not personal information about an identifiable individual: an organisation, a place, a date, a generic role, a program name, a statute.

*The question behind it:* Is there an identifiable individual behind this span at all?

Examples:

- Department of Health and Community Services, detected as a person.
- The Regional Director, with no name attached anywhere in the record.

Traps:

- A generic role in a small unit can identify one individual; where it does, it is not K6.

*Canada (federal):*

| Provision | Heading | Verification | Text or reason |
|---|---|---|---|
| Privacy Act, s. 3 | Definition of personal information | checked 2026-09-13 | "personal information means information about an identifiable individual that is recorded in any form." |

> K6 is not an exemption and not an exception to one. It records that the detector fired on something the definition does not reach. It is carried in the taxonomy so that a detector false positive is measured as a detector error rather than disappearing into the decision layer's accuracy.

*Newfoundland and Labrador:*

| Provision | Heading | Verification | Text or reason |
|---|---|---|---|
| Access to Information and Protection of Privacy Act, 2015, s. 2 | Definition of personal information | checked 2026-09-20 | ""personal information" means recorded information about an identifiable individual, including (i) the individual's name, address or telephone number, (ii) the individual's race, national or ethnic origin, colour, or religious or political beliefs or associations, (iii) the individual's age, sex, sexual orientation, marital status or family status, (iv) an identifying number, symbol or other particular assigned to the individual, (v) the individual's fingerprints, blood type or inheritable characteristics, (vi) information about the individual's health care status or history, including a physical or mental disability, (vii) information about the individual's educational, financial, criminal or employment status or history, (viii) the opinions of a person about the individual, and (ix) the individual's personal views or opinions, except where they are about someone else" |

> As federally, K6 records a detector false positive rather than an exemption.

### `E1`: Role undeterminable from the record

**Escalate.** The record does not say whether the individual is an official acting in an official capacity or a third party, and no rule and no model reached the confidence threshold. The proposal is to withhold; the reviewer is asked the role question.

*The question behind it:* Who is this person in this record?

Examples:

- A surname in a distribution list with no title, no letterhead match and no other mention in the record.

*Canada (federal):* An escalation is a question, not a provision. The record does not answer the role question, so no section can be cited yet. The reviewer's answer selects K2 or R1 and the schedule cites that code's provision.

*Newfoundland and Labrador:* Same as federally: an escalation is a question, so there is no provision to cite.

### `E2`: Mixed span the rules cannot sever cleanly

**Escalate.** A span containing more than one individual's information where the severance point is not determinable. The proposal is to withhold the whole span; the reviewer is asked where to cut.

*The question behind it:* Where does the requester's information end and the third party's begin?

*Canada (federal):*

| Provision | Heading | Verification | Text or reason |
|---|---|---|---|
| Access to Information Act, s. 25 | Severability | checked 2026-09-13 | "the head of the institution shall disclose any part of the record that does not contain, and can reasonably be severed from any part that contains, any such information or material." |

> E2 is escalated rather than decided precisely because section 25 requires a judgement about what can reasonably be severed, and "reasonably" is the reviewer's word, not the tool's.

*Newfoundland and Labrador:*

| Provision | Heading | Verification | Text or reason |
|---|---|---|---|
| Access to Information and Protection of Privacy Act, 2015, s. 8(2) | Right of access, severance | checked 2026-09-13 | "The right of access to a record does not extend to information excepted from disclosure under this Act, but if it is reasonable to sever that information from the record, an applicant has a right of access to the remainder of the record." |

### `E3`: Candidate non-personal exemption

**Flag only.** A block that may attract an exemption this tool does not decide: advice and recommendations, solicitor-client privilege, law enforcement, or a third party's business interests. Surfaced to the reviewer with the provision and no proposal. This tool decides personal-information questions; the rest is a different judgement.

*The question behind it:* Does one of these exemptions apply? This tool does not say.

Examples:

- A paragraph headed Recommendation in a briefing note.
- A paragraph marked Privileged and confidential, legal advice.

*Canada (federal):*

| Provision | Heading | Verification | Text or reason |
|---|---|---|---|
| Access to Information Act, s. 16 | Law enforcement and investigations | checked 2026-09-20 | "Law enforcement and investigations" |
| Access to Information Act, s. 20 | Third party information | checked 2026-09-20 | "Third party information" |
| Access to Information Act, s. 21 | Advice, etc. | checked 2026-09-20 | "Advice, etc." |
| Access to Information Act, s. 23 | Protected information - solicitors, advocates and notaries | checked 2026-09-20 | "Protected information - solicitors, advocates and notaries" |

> These four are flags with no proposal. They are in the taxonomy so that a reviewer reading a briefing note is not left to notice the advice exemption unaided, and so that the evaluation can report how often the flag was useful. The quote on each of these four is the marginal note, verbatim, and not the operative text of the section. That is what E3 cites, because E3 sends a reviewer to read the section rather than proposing anything under it, and quoting the whole of section 16 here would imply a precision this code does not have. Recorded explicitly so that "verified" is not read as more than it is. One typographic note, because a verbatim quote and this repository's punctuation rule collide exactly once. The marginal note of section 23 is printed with an em dash: "Protected information - solicitors, advocates and notaries" appears in the Act with an em dash where the hyphen is here. The words are unchanged.

*Newfoundland and Labrador:*

| Provision | Heading | Verification | Text or reason |
|---|---|---|---|
| Access to Information and Protection of Privacy Act, 2015, s. 29 | Policy advice or recommendations | checked 2026-09-20 | "Policy advice or recommendations" |
| Access to Information and Protection of Privacy Act, 2015, s. 30 | Legal advice | checked 2026-09-20 | "Legal advice" |
| Access to Information and Protection of Privacy Act, 2015, s. 31 | Disclosure harmful to law enforcement | checked 2026-09-20 | "Disclosure harmful to law enforcement" |
| Access to Information and Protection of Privacy Act, 2015, s. 39 | Disclosure harmful to business interests of a third party | checked 2026-09-20 | "Disclosure harmful to business interests of a third party" |

> NL also has a public-interest override at section 9 that can defeat a discretionary exception. This tool does not apply it and does not flag for it; that is recorded in docs/escalation.md as out of scope rather than left implicit.

## Where a jurisdiction decides a code differently

A code means the same question everywhere, but the statutes do not always
answer it the same way. Where they differ the jurisdiction says so here and
the tool behaves accordingly: this is not documentation of an intention, it
is the decision the pipeline applies for a span under that statute.

Every published number in this repository is the federal configuration, which
overrides nothing, so no result table is affected by the rows below.

| Jurisdiction | Code | Default | Under this statute | Why |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Newfoundland and Labrador | `K3` | keep | **escalate** | ATIPPA has no general publicly-available exception. Paragraph 40(2)(m) releases two enumerated things, attendance at a public event and receipt of an honour, and only where the disclosure is not contrary to the public interest under subsection (3). A name that is public for any other reason is not released by it, so the federal meaning of K3 has no equivalent here and the span goes to a person. |
| Newfoundland and Labrador | `K4` | keep | **escalate** | ATIPPA 40(5)(j) makes the time since a death a circumstance the head of a public body weighs and states no period, where the federal Act excludes a person dead more than twenty years from the definition outright. Releasing on a fixed number of years would perform a weighing the Act reserves to a person, against a threshold this project invented. |

## The statutes

**Canada (federal)**

- [Access to Information Act](https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/acts/A-1/) (R.S.C., 1985, c. A-1); consolidation read: 2026-07-21
- [Privacy Act](https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/acts/P-21/) (R.S.C., 1985, c. P-21); consolidation read: 2026-07-21

**Newfoundland and Labrador**

- [Access to Information and Protection of Privacy Act, 2015](https://www.assembly.nl.ca/legislation/sr/statutes/a01-2.htm) (SNL 2015, c. A-1.2); consolidation read: 2026 c16 s2, read 2026-09-20

## Adding a jurisdiction

Drop another YAML file into `sever/taxonomy/` beside `federal.yaml`. It declares
its statutes, then answers every code in `categories.yaml`: either with the
provisions that carry it, or by naming it in `unmapped` with the reason the Act
has no equivalent. The loader refuses a file that leaves a code unanswered, and
refuses a provision that claims nothing about whether it was checked.

Where the new Act answers a code differently from `categories.yaml`, set
`decision` on that code's mapping and say why in `decision_reason`. The loader
refuses an override with no reason, because the override changes what is released
and the reason is what a reviewer reads. Expect to need it rarely: a code whose
decision changes between jurisdictions is usually two codes wearing one name.
